results.description: Menemerus bivittatus (Dufour, 1831), female. 3rd Lane off Nagoda Road, Kalutara, Sri Lanka. A pantropical salticid that is often encountered on tree trunks in gardens, outer walls of buildings, etc.

default_photo.attribution: (c) Kim Moore, all rights reserved, uploaded by Kim Moore

identifications.body:
I feel less certain about the species level identity of this specimen now! There seem to be at least 2-3 more species of Menemerus in addition to Menemerus bivittatus in Sri Lanka. Benjamin et al (2012) list Menemerus bivittatus and Menemerus fulvus as occurring in Sri Lanka and there is a speccimen of Menemerus nigli from Sri Lanka recorded on http://www.jumping-spiders.com/.

The specimen in this observation might be a subadult female.

results.description: Chrysilla sp., near Chrysilla lauta (Araneae: Salticidae). 3rd Lane off Nagoda Road, Kalutara, Sri Lanka. The name "Chrysilla lauta" seems to be used on the internet for 2 different Chrysilla species, based on color pattern. The present photographs from Kalutara, Sri Lanka, agree with this: https://twitter.com/Sahelanth/status/747814598468898817 but not with this: https://twitter.com/l1ght3n/status/544679447341723648

default_photo.attribution: (c) Manjunath Acharya, some rights reserved (CC BY-NC), uploaded by Manjunath Acharya

comments.body: Going by distribution could be https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/627063-Phintella-volupe

Thank you @vijaybarve @ruwangika @tigerbb @thilinahettiarachchi I had forgotten all about this observation - from the steps of my wife's home in Kalutara! My notes in the 'Description' were written at the time, long before the following paper which clarified the taxonomy of Chrysilla & related salticids in S Asia:

Kanesharatnam, N. & Benjamin, S.P. 2019. Multilocus genetic and morphological phylogenetic analysis reveals a radiation of shiny South Asian jumping spiders (Araneae, Salticidae). ZooKeys 839: 1-81. https://doi.org/10.3897/zookeys.839.28312
I just had that thought, you have forgotten this sighting. Very beautiful critter..! And very interesting about your sense on most of species since very long time ago where resources were not ad-lib.

comments.body: @bothrops07 Is this the same weird spider that i uploaded a few days ago?

I'm not sure about this. The white dots on the abdomen might indicate N. acerba (known from Texas, but not Louisiana , but the carapace does look like N. pulex. It does appear to be immature and the patterns of immatures are not well known.

comments.body:
I *think* this is a Habronattus decorus male, but I am not sure. @b_coulter @tigerbb ?
Compare with this recent post on Bug Guide:
http://bugguide.net/node/view/1356737

Boy, they sure can be similar! I've pored over many a resource on the two but am not coming up with enough to confidently ID this specimen. I am leaning towards viridipes, however, mostly because of the sort-of crown line on the head, the red face (also seen in a few BG decorus images but more prevalent in viridipes), and less yellow coloration of the femurs. Here's a pretty similar example: http://bugguide.net/node/view/80224/bgimage

Cool, thanks for weighing in, @tigerbb . Those head markings are quite striking and the two species are very similar. I am learning lots through such discussions. Let's see what others say. Great shots, @christine123 !

Great discussion and thanks you two. I had some trouble with this one but settled on H. viridipes for many of the reasons noted. But I am no expert on jumping spiders so am very keen to hear what others might also say.
